public_rationale: The May 29, 2024 paper describes how training-data access helps auditors trace problems and assess fair use [e1]. The September 17, 2024 study identifies linguistic discrimination in model responses through output-based evaluation [e2]. The February 21, 2026 study traces selected, marked training data through outputs under black-box access [e3]. These findings show benefits of data access and some investigation possible without disclosure, but do not isolate disclosure’s effect on assessing societal bias, the extent of creator exploitation, or outside mitigation effectiveness [e1–e3]. The full causal claim remains unresolved [e1–e3].
limitations: Output discrimination does not establish bias propagation through society under widespread use [e2].
Tracing selected training examples does not establish the extent of unauthorized or uncompensated use or resulting harm to creators [e3].
The evidence does not quantify how much training-data secrecy impairs outside mitigation or isolate it from other access restrictions [e1–e3].

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that training-data secrecy prevents reliable assessment of propagated biases and the extent of creator exploitation, and substantially weakens independent risk mitigation.
Identifying particular biased outputs or particular training examples is relevant counterevidence, but does not by itself establish societal effects or the extent of exploitation.
Creator exploitation includes uncompensated or unauthorized use and resulting harm; identifying dataset membership alone does not establish either legal infringement or economic harm.
This is a general causal claim, so later research may test its mechanism. It is not scored as a forecast conditional on a particular deployment.
criteria.support_condition: Independent audits or comparative studies show that withholding training-data information prevents the stated assessments and materially reduces outside mitigation effectiveness, with disclosure addressing those limitations.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Independent investigators reliably assess the stated societal biases and extent of creator exploitation without training-data disclosure, or comparisons show that nondisclosure does not substantially impair outside mitigation. Evidence settling only one component would warrant a component-level finding.

evidence.excerpt: Access to data helps auditors trace problems and assess fair use.
evidence.explanation: The paper identifies concrete audit benefits from access to training data, supporting the proposed mechanism. It does not establish that nondisclosure prevents all the claimed assessments or quantify a substantial effect on every outside mitigation effort.

Researchers identified discrimination by prompting the models and evaluating their responses. This challenges the reading that no bias can be identified without dataset disclosure, but does not measure propagation through society under widespread deployment.

The study demonstrates tracing selected, marked data through generated outputs without internal model access. This limits an absolute impossibility claim, but does not establish the full extent of creators’ uncompensated use or harm.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Independent comparative audits with and without training-data disclosure, holding access to weights, deployment records, and developer assistance constant, that measure reliable assessment of societal bias and creator exploitation and the effectiveness of outside mitigation.
